title: Birthstones by Month
description: Traditional and modern birthstones for every month, with a quick-reference table and a short section on the history and lore of each January to December gem.
html:
Wearing a stone tied to your birth month is one of the oldest and most popular customs in the gem world. Some people wear theirs for sentiment, others because they believe it brings luck, protection or a particular quality. The tradition has shifted over the centuries, and lists differ depending on the country and the jeweler you ask. This guide sets out the traditional and modern stones for every month, a quick-reference table and a short section on each stone and what practitioners associate with it.

Where birthstones come from

The idea is often traced back to the breastplate of the Jewish high priest described in the Book of Exodus, which carried twelve stones. Later writers linked those twelve stones to the months of the year and to the zodiac signs. By the eighteenth century, people in Poland and Germany were already wearing a stone for their birth month. In the United States, the National Association of Jewellers published an official list in 1912, which has been updated several times since, most recently adding stones such as spinel and tanzanite.

Traditional versus modern lists

Traditional lists reflect older customs and often include stones that are less expensive or more widely available in ancient times, such as bloodstone and sardonyx. Modern lists were designed partly for the jewelry trade and favour transparent gems that look good in a ring. Many months now have two or three choices, so you can pick the one that fits your taste and your budget.

Birthstones at a glance

MonthTraditionalModern
JanuaryGarnetGarnet
FebruaryAmethystAmethyst
MarchBloodstoneAquamarine
AprilDiamondDiamond
MayEmeraldEmerald
JunePearlPearl, Moonstone, Alexandrite
JulyRubyRuby
AugustSardonyxPeridot, Spinel
SeptemberSapphireSapphire
OctoberOpalOpal, Tourmaline
NovemberTopazTopaz, Citrine
DecemberTurquoiseTurquoise, Zircon, Tanzanite

January: Garnet

Garnet is best known in deep red, though the family spans orange, green and even color-changing varieties. Its name likely comes from the Latin for pomegranate, because the crystals resemble the fruit's seeds. Practitioners link garnet with energy, commitment and steady passion, and call it a stone for staying motivated through dark winter months. Hardness runs 6.5 to 7.5.

February: Amethyst

Amethyst is a purple quartz whose name comes from a Greek word meaning not drunken. Ancient Greeks wore it, and drinking cups were sometimes carved from it, in the belief that it kept a clear head. In the crystal tradition, it is linked with calm, restful sleep and intuition. Its color can fade in strong sun.

March: Aquamarine and Bloodstone

Aquamarine is a pale sea-blue beryl, and its name means water of the sea in Latin. Sailors reportedly carried it for safe passage. Practitioners associate it with calm communication and a soothing, clear mind. The traditional March stone, Bloodstone, is a dark green chalcedony with red flecks, long linked with courage and endurance.

April: Diamond

Diamond is the hardest natural substance known, at 10 on the Mohs scale, and its Greek-derived name means unconquerable. It is a symbol of clarity, lasting commitment and resilience. In crystal circles it is treated as an amplifier of intention, and it is also the stone of the sixtieth wedding anniversary.

May: Emerald

Emerald is the green variety of beryl, colored by chromium and vanadium. It has been prized since ancient Egypt, and the mines of Colombia and Zambia are still famous. Practitioners associate it with love, loyalty, growth and a calm heart. Most emeralds are filled with oil, so avoid ultrasonic cleaners and harsh soaps.

June: Pearl, Moonstone and Alexandrite

June has three. Pearl is an organic gem formed inside mollusks and has long stood for purity and wisdom. Moonstone glows with a floating, silvery light and is linked to intuition and emotional balance. Alexandrite is a rare chrysoberyl that shifts from green in daylight to red in incandescent light, and it is associated with adaptability and joy. Pearls are soft and easily damaged by perfume.

July: Ruby

Ruby is red corundum, colored by chromium, and one of the hardest gems at Mohs 9. Burmese rubies are especially famous. Many cultures wore it for vitality and courage, and practitioners link it to passion, confidence and a warm heart.

August: Peridot, Spinel and Sardonyx

Peridot is a lime-to-olive green gem formed deep in the earth and sometimes found in meteorites. Egyptians mined it on an island in the Red Sea. It is associated with renewal, generosity and a cheerful outlook. Spinel, long mistaken for ruby, was added as a modern birthstone and is linked to energy and recovery from tiredness. Sardonyx, a banded red and white chalcedony, is the traditional choice and is linked to courage.

September: Sapphire

Sapphire is the blue variety of corundum, though it occurs in nearly every color except red. The finest blue stones come from Kashmir, Burma and Sri Lanka. Tradition links sapphire to wisdom, loyalty and mental focus, and it was favoured by clergy and kings. Mohs 9.

October: Opal and Tourmaline

Opal displays flashes of spectral color called play-of-color and is mostly sourced from Australia and Ethiopia. It is linked to creativity and emotional expression, and it is soft and water-containing, so protect it from heat and dryness. Tourmaline comes in more colors than almost any gem. Pink and watermelon varieties are favourites, and many people associate it with balance and protection.

November: Topaz and Citrine

Topaz naturally occurs in golden, pink, blue and clear varieties, and much of the vivid blue sold today is irradiated or heat-treated. It is associated with warmth, generosity and self-expression. Citrine is the yellow quartz known as the merchant's stone, and it is associated with abundance and optimism. Natural citrine is rare, and most commercial pieces are heated amethyst.

December: Turquoise, Zircon and Tanzanite

Turquoise is a blue-green copper aluminum phosphate that has been used for thousands of years across Persia, Egypt and the American Southwest. It is linked to protection and travel, and it is soft and porous. Zircon is a brilliant natural gem, unrelated to the synthetic cubic zirconia. Tanzanite is a violet-blue zoisite found only near Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and was added to the list in 2002. It is associated with intuition and spiritual awareness.

Choosing which birthstone to wear

You do not have to choose the stone for your own month. Some people wear the stone for their zodiac sign, a loved one's birth month or whichever one they feel drawn to. A few practical guidelines help:

  • Check hardness before choosing a ring. Diamond, ruby and sapphire survive daily wear, while pearl, opal and turquoise need gentle treatment.
  • Ask whether the stone has been heated, dyed, oiled or irradiated. Many are, and good sellers will tell you. See our guide to spotting fakes.
  • Keep soft and porous stones away from water. Our water safety guide lists which ones.
  • If you like the idea of astrology, see our zodiac crystals guide for a different way to choose.

Birthstone traditions are cultural and personal, and crystals complement but never replace professional medical care.
